newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds marked up on bullish EMU sentiment.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds marked up on bullish EMU sentiment.

text.p: Irish bonds were marked up on Monday in line with other European bond markets, buoyed by last week's strong performance and by the growing belief that EMU will start on time because of the over-riding political will, dealers said.
"Markets are all bullish at present," a dealer said. "Last week's positive sentiment has carried over and the feeling out of Amsterdam is that EMU will start on schedule."
However, thin trade on Monday suggested a degree of investor wariness remained, he added.
By 1500 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 28 pence at 102.20 to yield 5.90 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 35 pence at 109.90 to yield 6.52 percent.
Irish bonds were outperforming Germany, dealers said, with yields against German Bunds narrowing to 155 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 85 over in the 10-year.

With few economic numbers to go on today and conflicting reports coming out of the Amsterdam summit, players are increasingly taking their positions on the basis that EMU will start on schedule -- despite tension between France and Germany over the stability pact and a possible jobs protocol.

"Markets are anticipating some agreement in Amsterdam and that EMU will remain on track," a dealer said. "In point of fact though, I think most of the EMU convergence has already happened -- we're now looking at the fundamentals."
Looking ahead, traders are eyeing the U.S. consumer price index, particularly the core figure excluding food and energy, which is due tomorrow.
The data is expected to show little sign of inflationary pressure and so should add to last week's market-friendly figures out of the U.S.
In the U.K., the main number of the week is retail sales on Wednesday, with analysts forecasting a rise in May against April of 0.3 percent
Dealers said tomorrow's NTMA auction of 80 million Irish pounds of the eight percent bond due 2006 should attract non-resident interest.
